title: The Investment Consequences Of The US-Canada Trade Spat
gist: Louis-Vincent Gave argues the consensus reading of Canada's walk-away from a US trade deal — bearish loonie, bearish Canadian assets — is right only tactically; the lasting consequence is that Mark Carney can now use the 'patriotic card' to steamroll domestic opposition to pipelines, railroads and LNG terminals, funded by the CAD2.5trn 'Big Nine' pension complex repatriating capital from the US. Add a possible re-opening of Chinese demand for Canadian assets, frozen since the Meng Wanzhou arrest, and the long-term setup is bullish Canadian commodity producers and the Canadian dollar.

insights.claim: The US trade deal Canada rejected required Canada to essentially turn its back on China, which would have reduced Canada to an economic dominion of the United States — making refusal a sovereignty decision rather than a narrow trade calculation.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Frames the spat as structural and durable, not a haggle that gets patched up in a quarter — position for a prolonged reordering of Canadian trade rather than a quick reconciliation trade.
insights.quote: The deal the US put on the table, one which involved Canada essentially turning its back on China, a rapidly growing trade partner, would have left Canada as essentially an economic dominion of the United States.
insights.locator: The first, and strongest, explanation

insights.claim: Any concession Canada makes to Washington today carries no settled value, because the US could next demand severing ties with Europe or Brazil depending on presidential mood — so the option value of refusing exceeds the option value of agreeing.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for pricing any US bilateral deal in this era: treat US commitments as revocable options, which raises the required concession discount for every counterparty negotiating with Washington.
insights.quote: if Canada agreed today to sever economic ties with China, who is to say what the US might ask for tomorrow?
insights.locator: After all, if Canada agreed today

insights.claim: USMCA was renegotiated out of NAFTA only seven years ago and was described by Trump at the time as the best of deals, establishing that a signed US trade agreement has a shelf life measured in single-digit years.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Trade-agreement durability should be discounted in cross-border capex models; supply chains built on treaty permanence carry an unpriced re-negotiation risk.
insights.quote: the USMCA agreement was renegotiated from Nafta just seven years ago and at the time, Trump described it as the best of deals
insights.locator: After all, the USMCA agreement was renegotiated

insights.claim: Carney's line that 'sometimes the US signature is written in pencil' is the durable framing of this episode and will shape how other US counterparties negotiate.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Watch for the same rhetoric migrating to EU, Japanese and Korean negotiators — it lowers the political cost of refusing US terms and raises the odds of more walk-aways.
insights.quote: we recognized that sometimes the US signature is written in pencil
insights.locator: In that regards, Carney's quip

insights.claim: Canadian leaders are diverging from European ones in trade posture, with Carney walking away from a deal European leaders in the same position accepted.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: The Canada-Europe divergence is a live test of whether resisting US terms is punished or rewarded by markets — the relative performance of Canadian vs European cyclical assets becomes the scoreboard.
insights.quote: Unlike European leaders, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney elected to walk away from what he felt was a bad trade deal for his country.
insights.locator: Unlike European leaders

insights.claim: Ontario — Canada's industrial heartland and the core base of Carney's Liberal Party — will likely absorb the bulk of the economic fallout from the trade breakdown, putting the government's own electoral base at risk.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: The pain is regionally concentrated in manufacturing, not spread evenly — short Ontario-levered industrials and autos while the commodity-producing West is the offsetting long.
insights.quote: Ontario, the industrial heartland of Canada but also the core base of Carney’s Liberal Party, will likely bear the brunt of the economic fallout
insights.locator: In time, this could end up having an important political cost

insights.claim: Standing up to perceived US bullying is politically positive for Carney in the short term even as the economic costs build, which means the political feedback loop will not force a rapid reversal.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Do not underwrite a quick capitulation trade — the near-term domestic incentive runs toward escalation, so the spat likely persists past the point of economic rationality.
insights.locator: The second explanation might be politically driven

insights.claim: Canadian imports of US capital and industrial goods — planes, Caterpillar machines, chemical products — stand at record highs while consumer product imports have dropped clearly over the past 18 months, evidencing a consumer-led boycott rather than a broad trade collapse.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: The exposure is in US consumer brands selling into Canada, not in industrial exporters — screen for US staples and discretionary names with meaningful Canadian revenue rather than assuming uniform trade-war damage.
insights.quote: while Canadian imports of US goods (whether planes, Caterpillar machines, chemical products etc…) stand at record highs, the past 18 months have witnessed a clear drop in the imports of consumer products
insights.locator: A defiance against US products which is starting to come through in the data

insights.claim: The consumer boycott is grassroots and cultural rather than policy-driven — illustrated by an elderly shopper on Vancouver Island telling the author he could not buy oranges because they came from California — which makes it slower to reverse than a tariff.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Bottom-up boycotts outlive the political dispute that started them; assume a multi-year impairment of US brand equity in Canada even if tariffs are lifted.
insights.quote: you can’t buy these. They are from California!
insights.locator: As I was picking up oranges

themes.theme: Infrastructure Unlock As The Silver Lining

insights.claim: Canada's core comparative advantage is extracting oil, natural gas, gold, wheat and potash in a jurisdiction investors are broadly comfortable with, but it has been particularly incompetent at building the export infrastructure needed to monetize that advantage internationally.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: The bull case for Canadian resource equities is a logistics story, not a reserves story — the re-rating trigger is permits and pipe, not commodity price alone.
insights.quote: Canada’s main comparative advantage is to get things out of the ground (whether oil, natural gas, gold, wheat, potash...) in a jurisdiction investors feel broadly comfortable with.
insights.locator: This shift in Canadian attitudes to the US could have a silver lining

insights.claim: Lacking an Alberta-to-BC-ports oil pipeline and Maritimes LNG terminals, Canadian producers have been forced to sell oil, electricity and natural gas at a discount into the only easily accessible market — the US — so the discount is a structural transport problem, not a quality one.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Every kilometre of new export capacity compresses the Canadian price discount directly into producer margins — the highest-torque exposure is to differential-sensitive Canadian oil and gas names.
insights.quote: Canadian producers have had to sell discounted oil, electricity or natural gas to the only easily accessible market, namely the US
insights.locator: Instead, Canadian producers have had to sell discounted oil

insights.claim: By shutting the American door and wrapping himself in the Maple-Leaf flag, Carney can now use the patriotic card to steamroll the Greens, First Nations and NDP local governments that have blocked pipelines, railroads and LNG terminals.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: This is the central non-consensus call: the trade rupture is the political unlock for Canadian infrastructure that a decade of economic argument could not deliver — watch permit approvals as the confirming signal.
insights.quote: Mark Carney can now steamroll anyone standing in the way of the much-needed infrastructure roll-out with the “patriotic card.”
insights.locator: Essentially, Mark Carney can now steamroll anyone

insights.claim: The outcome is explicitly binary: if the infrastructure roll-out happens Carney is a consequential prime minister, and if it does not, the combination of no infrastructure and a broken US relationship leaves Canada in tough economic binds.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Treat Canadian exposure as a bimodal bet with a clear observable trigger — size positions for two very different outcomes rather than a blended base case.
insights.quote: High stakes…
insights.locator: If he manages to do so, Carney could still go down

insights.claim: Canada's 'Big Nine' pension funds — CPPIB, La Caisse, BCI, AIMCO and Ontario Teachers among them — collectively manage roughly CAD2.5trn with an estimated half deployed in the US, making them the single largest potential funding source for domestic infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Roughly CAD1.25trn sits in US assets — even a modest repatriation shift is a large, mechanical bid for CAD and Canadian real assets and a marginal seller of US ones.
insights.quote: The “Big Nine” Canadian pension funds (i.e. CPPIB, La Caisse, BCI, AIMCO, Ontario Teachers…) collectively manage around CAD2.5trn and it is estimated that around half of that money is deployed in the US.
insights.locator: Another interesting angle to the US-Canada spat

insights.claim: The binding constraint on funding Canadian infrastructure has never been capital availability but political will — Canadian capital very much exists, and pension funds would prefer deploying it at home if given the opportunity.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Removes the usual 'where does the money come from' objection to the Canadian infrastructure thesis — the gating item is policy news flow, which can re-rate assets far faster than a financing cycle.
insights.quote: What has lacked so far has been the political will to make this happen. If the political will is now found, capital could return to Canada, instead of constantly leaving.
insights.locator: The reality is that Canadian capital very much exists

insights.claim: Canadian pension allocation to the US reflects the unmatched depth of US capital markets rather than any bearish view on Canada, so the repatriation impulse is political and can shift faster than the underlying market-structure rationale.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Political catalysts can override structural allocation logic — monitor pension fund public statements on domestic allocation as an early tell for the loonie.
insights.quote: This asset allocation mostly reflects the fact that the US offers a depth of capital markets that no other country can match.
insights.locator: This asset allocation mostly reflects the fact

themes.theme: Trade The Timeframe: Loonie Short-Term vs Long-Term

insights.claim: Weekend financial media consensus holds that the US-Canada trade spat is inherently bearish for the Canadian dollar and Canadian assets — a view the author accepts only for the coming weeks, not the long run.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: The explicit trade is to fade the consensus over a multi-quarter horizon while respecting it tactically — near-term weakness is the entry point, not the thesis.
insights.quote: the consensus take seems to be that the US-Canadian trade spat is inherently bearish for the Canadian dollar and Canadian assets
insights.locator: From a quick glance across the weekend's financial media

insights.claim: Because the loonie and Canadian assets are cyclical, they may well trade on the heavy side over the coming weeks before the infrastructure and repatriation dynamics assert themselves.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: An explicit sequencing call: expect near-term CAD and Canadian equity weakness, and treat it as accumulation rather than confirmation of the bear case.
insights.quote: over the coming weeks, Canadian asset prices, and the loonie, may well trade on the heavy side
insights.locator: So, to the extent that the Canadian dollar

insights.claim: If the trade spat delivers the electroshock that finally gets commodity infrastructure built and pension funds repatriate US assets to fund it, the long-term impact is very bullish for Canadian commodity-producing assets and the Canadian dollar.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: The core trade expression: long Canadian commodity producers and CAD on a multi-year view, conditional on observable permitting and pension allocation milestones.
insights.quote: the longer-term impact should then prove to be very bullish for Canadian commodity-producing assets, and for the Canadian dollar
insights.locator: But over the long term, if the current trade spat

insights.claim: From the US side the timing of this trade war is poor, coming alongside a looming US-China summit and the unfolding consequences of the US-Iran war including soaring diesel prices and rising freight costs.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Stacked simultaneous shocks — Canada trade, China summit, Iran war energy inflation — argue for higher US inflation and logistics costs, and reduce Washington's leverage to sustain the fight.
insights.quote: this trade war is also poorly timed given the looming US-China summit, and the unfolding consequences of the US-Iran war (i.e. soaring diesel prices, rising freight costs...)
insights.locator: From a US standpoint, this trade war is also poorly timed

insights.claim: Chinese investors were keen buyers of Canadian assets until 2018 — to the point Vancouver was nicknamed Hongcouver — but that appetite stalled with the arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou and the perception that Canada would always side with the US against China.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, datable shutdown of a foreign bid — meaning there is a known pool of dormant demand that can return rather than needing to be created.
insights.quote: it’s not for nothing that Vancouver is sometimes referred to as Hongcouver
insights.locator: Finally, another interesting angle to Mark Carney's decision

insights.claim: Carney slamming the door on Trump changes how China and the wider world perceive Canada's alignment, potentially restoring a Chinese and broader foreign bid for the loonie and Canadian assets.
insights.speaker: Louis-Vincent Gave
insights.so_what: An under-priced second-order kicker to the CAD bull case — watch Chinese direct investment and Vancouver/Toronto real asset flows as the confirming evidence.
insights.quote: To the extent that this perception now shifts again, the loonie could suddenly find a Chinese, and foreign, bid once again?
insights.locator: This made Canadian assets a lot less attractive to Chinese buyers
